/docs/README.mainHtml:
Claus Network

Claus Network gives developers and agents a shared project identity, scoped access, reproducible source records and a path toward reviewed contract changes. A project does not need a token.

The public API supports authentication, projects, delegated agents, source publication, bounded Solidity compilation and sponsored reviews for admitted pilots. The public graph reads explicitly published project records. API 0.10.5 also exposes the protected Sepolia workflow, services, project wallets, isolated publication, the vault interface, signed operator transfers, the disabled inference interface and the contract-request profile for one admitted Sepolia reference. Operational activation is reported separately by /health. See release status before building against a capability.

Start a project without launching a token. The current delivery focuses on project continuity, agent access, services and controlled contract changes. New token launches are deferred to a later phase.

Use your own editor, agent or command line. The website is an explorer; it is not required for authorization or project work.

  • API
  • Public graph
  • Contract candidate
  • Start a project

The intended upgrade path is: pin the exact source, build it, collect independent evidence, obtain a scoped Claus decision, then execute the exact approved change. An IMD report is evidence for a decision. It is not itself permission to change a contract.

/docs/clients.mainHtml:
MCP, SDK and CLI

All clients use the same service and authorization checks. A different transport does not add permissions.

HTTP MCP

Endpoint: https://claus-network-api.vercel.app/mcp.

Use a client that supports Streamable HTTP, protocol version 2025-06-18, and a protected bearer-token configuration. Requests are JSON-RPC POSTs with Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json, text/event-stream. GET streaming is not enabled; the server is stateless between HTTP requests.

tools/list exposes the implemented operations. Tool calls return structured results or isError: true. Check this flag even when the HTTP response is successful.

Credential creation, login-session creation and credential rotation are deliberately absent from model-facing tools. Bootstrap them using the API or CLI so raw credentials do not appear in a model's tool output. OAuth discovery and browser-driven OAuth are not currently implemented.

JavaScript SDK

The reference client is interfaces/sdk.mjs in the source distribution:

import { createClient } from './interfaces/sdk.mjs';

const client = createClient({
  origin: 'https://claus-network-api.vercel.app',
  token: process.env.CLAUS_NETWORK_TOKEN
});
const projects = await client.call('project_list', {});

The SDK and CLI default to https://claus-network-api.vercel.app. Set origin or CLAUS_NETWORK_URL explicitly when using another operator. Provide secrets through a protected environment or secret manager. The SDK uses HTTPS, refuses redirects for API calls, encodes resource IDs and does not automatically retry mutations. Errors include a code and HTTP status. An HTML page or other non-JSON response produces invalid_api_response; its contents are not included in the error.

CLI

Use Node 24.14 or later in the Node 24 line. From the source distribution:

node interfaces/cli.mjs --help
node interfaces/cli.mjs operations
node interfaces/cli.mjs describe service_register

operations lists the bundled API operations as JSON. describe returns an operation's exact input schema, route, authentication requirement and whether its response needs a private credential file. Both commands run offline without reading credentials. Their apiVersion identifies the bundled schema, not the current server release. Listing an operation does not mean it is enabled for your project; consult the live service status and capability endpoint.

To make a request:

export CLAUS_NETWORK_URL=https://claus-network-api.vercel.app
export CLAUS_NETWORK_TOKEN_FILE=/absolute/private/path/token
node interfaces/cli.mjs call project_list

For an operation with input, add the path of a JSON file. For operations that return a new token, set CLAUS_NETWORK_NEW_TOKEN_FILE to a new private file path. The CLI creates it exclusively with mode 0600 before making the request and does not print the secret. A pending-response marker means the outcome needs recovery; it is not a usable token.

If a credential rotation loses its response, the previous key may already be revoked. Keep the pending file and the original mandate ID; do not repeat the rotation with a different output file. Use a valid owner session to revoke that mandate, then create a new mandate and credential with the intended scopes and expiry. Existing files are never overwritten, including when a command is repeated after an interruption. Never paste a token or signed login response into a model conversation.

Discovery and error recovery

capabilities is public. project_capabilities, identity_list and resource_list recover scoped rights, identity metadata and existing IDs. Operation descriptions appear in OpenAPI and MCP. Owner-policy operations never become agent permissions.

A 429 response includes Retry-After; wait before retrying reads. capacity_reached means an admission limit has been reached, not that a payment is required. Authentication, permission, state conflict, funding, provider and temporary service errors remain distinguishable by the stable error code. Do not replay mutations under new keys after a timeout. Read the original resource and retain the input, key and any pending credential file.

/docs/contract-intake.mainHtml:
Contract requests

Since API 0.10.1, the network implements an asynchronous contract-request profile. On 12 October 2026, its verified Inbox and separate dispatcher were activated for one explicitly admitted Claus-owned Sepolia project. The first finalized request received a genuine Claus approval. Its original 200,000-gas reference receiver failed to accept the callback; the stored Inbox result and queued upgrade remain intact. The canonical result has been recovered into the source-verified replacement receiver, with finalized chain readback. The original queued upgrade has finalized; its temporary binding and mandate are revoked. This is not public enrollment. Existing API clients can continue to submit proposals directly. See the activation receipt.

Flow

  1. An authorized project owner or agent creates a binding through contract_binding_create, using API, SDK or CLI. It names one requester contract, an expiry and a maximum request count. The host pins the inbox, its deployed code, chain and capability. Binding creation requires contract.request and proposal.create. The complete protected-change workflow additionally needs proposal.execute, proposal.read, review.read and artifact.read, together with current project and sponsor admission. Granting a binding alone does not grant these other capabilities.
  2. That contract calls ClausRequestInbox.request with the returned onchainBinding, capability, deadline, callback gas and UTF-8 JSON input. The initial input contains exactly moduleId and configuration. It requests a configuration change to a previously reviewed module, not an arbitrary call, purchase or new deployment.
  3. A worker reads finalized canonical events, checks current grants and creates the existing proposal workflow under a deterministic ID. Unknown bindings create no project work. A replay or lost response keeps the same proposal.
  4. The existing review and Claus decision process runs. The returned result explicitly says proposal-decision. An approval result does not say that its subsequent contract execution is complete.
  5. An admitted dispatcher records the result hash and evidence hash in the inbox. The requester can receive onClausResult(bytes32,uint8,bytes,bytes32). Failed callbacks can be retried with the identical result; a successful callback is delivered once.

No website is required. There are four shared interface operations: binding creation, binding lookup, binding revocation and request lookup. Revocation stops new work; it does not undo a proposal or transaction already dispatched. Completed results remain available to authorized readers.

Client example

The reference client prepares calls for the source-verified ClausRequestClient contract. Use your own admitted project, deployed requester and controller. The live reference's requester belongs to Claus; its address is not a shared gateway for other projects.

Create the binding with your existing authenticated SDK client. Store the exact body and returned ID before continuing; reuse them when recovering a lost response.

const binding = await api.call('contract_binding_create', {
  projectId,
  requester: pin.requester,
  expiresAt, // fixed future Unix timestamp in milliseconds
  maxRequests: 1,
  idempotencyKey: 'my-contract-binding-1'
});

pin contains chainId, inbox, codeHash (the Inbox runtime hash), requester, requesterCodeHash and controller. Obtain these from the admitted deployment and your verified requester deployment, not from untrusted model output. chain is a viem public client for Sepolia; api is the authenticated network SDK client.

import {
  prepareContractRequest,
  locateContractRequest
} from './reference/contract-request-client.mjs';

const prepared = await prepareContractRequest({
  api, chain, projectId, bindingId: binding.id, pin,
  input: { moduleId, configuration },
  deadline // fixed future Unix timestamp in seconds, before binding expiry
});

Preparation rereads the binding, checks both finalized runtimes and the requester controller, reads its 1,000,000-gas callback budget, then simulates the call. The returned preparation binds that budget. Earlier saved 200,000-gas preparations remain readable, but the legacy receiver is not used for fresh requests. It returns prepared.transaction with the exact chain, sender, recipient, data and zero value. It does not sign, fund or send. Use your existing durable wallet tooling to select gas and nonce, sign and submit once. Preserve the signed transaction hash before broadcast. A lost response requires reconciliation of that hash, not another call to submit.

Save prepared alongside that original hash. Read its actual event to locate the network request:

const located = await locateContractRequest({
  chain, prepared, transactionHash: originalTransactionHash
});
const result = await api.call('contract_request_get', {
  projectId, requestId: located.requestId
});

The event lookup checks the canonical block, Inbox runtime, requester, binding and exact input. located.finalized describes the transaction's chain status. A network 404 before the finalized event is indexed means continue reading the same request ID; it is not a reason to submit again. If indexing does not appear, inspect the binding's latestRejection: a skipped concurrent request is not queued for later execution. A returned proposal-decision can be read through proposal_get to follow its separate execution and any accepted project delay. Finish by revoking the binding with contract_binding_revoke and retiring any temporary agent mandate.

Public data and limits

Contract input, requester, result and evidence hashes are public. Do not include credentials, private source or personal information. Only the small decision receipt is returned; private review text is excluded. Input and output are bounded to 8 KiB; callback gas is bounded and the target is always the requester. The inbox cannot receive a user-supplied callback target or arbitrary value transfer.

The inbox is immutable. The dispatcher is fixed at deployment and can resolve only pending requests before their deadlines. A requester can cancel; anyone can expire an overdue request. A callback's result bytes must match the stored result hash. Consumers must authenticate the inbox address and its admitted deployment before trusting any callback.

Evidence and remaining release work

Solidity tests cover cancellation, expiry, callback failure/retry, reentrancy, replay and size/gas boundaries. The local EVM integration deploys actual bytecode, reads a finalized event, creates one proposal and delivers its result to a real receiver through the budgeted dispatcher. Both lost broadcast responses are recovered after restart using the original transactions. That local test uses a labelled synthetic decision; it is not a real Claus review or an independent audit.

The scanner preserves its canonical cursor across restarts, and the delivery coordinator preserves the original delivery ID. Turning off intake stops new submissions while still allowing existing deliveries to be reconciled. The separate dispatcher enforces the exact inbox, result, current grant, a cumulative gas budget and original transaction identity. Reservation and wallet locking are atomic. Budget is released only on final settlement or cancellation before broadcast; revocation still permits read-only reconciliation. One automated callback attempt is sponsored, and a failed callback can subsequently be retried onchain by its caller.

A broader release requires a genuine end-to-end decision/callback run in addition to the independent assessment, source-verified Inbox, bounded dispatcher and explicit capability admission. None of the endpoints, fixture receipts or a database flag alone proves completion. Check release status.

The hosted worker, exact API deployment pin, seven-day one-project budget and Inbox admission are installed for the bounded Sepolia reference. The lifetime dispatcher gas ceiling is 0.0002 Sepolia ETH, with no automatic refill. The original independent inbox review is complete. The assessment retains all ten repository findings and accepts only the exact Inbox and bounded owner-operated Sepolia pilot. The provider Markdown endpoint returned 503, so the worker retained the officially accepted judge submission, its complete findings and its provenance. No replacement order or payment was created.

The admitted capability lists exact pilot project IDs. A project outside that list cannot create a binding or start a queued proposal. Removing a project also prevents a newly signed delivery from being broadcast; an already broadcast transaction retains its original hash and accounting. Intake health requires the admitted worker release and exact inbox generation, so a stale worker cannot report the new deployment as ready.

Source 0.9.3 isolates withdrawn projects and old inbox bindings in the scanner. A pending wallet slot or exhausted signing budget defers new deliveries without preventing existing transactions from being reconciled. The optional ClausRequestClient is an operator-owned reference: only its controller submits or cancels, and its pinned inbox supplies the canonical decision. It holds no funds and does not execute the decision. The client has local tests; it is not part of the independent inbox audit.

A requester can cancel while a request is pending, including after offchain work has started. Cancellation does not refund spent sponsor funds, restore the binding request count, or erase an existing offchain proposal. A cancellation ordered before resolution can prevent an onchain result and waste the bounded resolution gas. The first pilot accepts this limitation with one explicitly admitted project, one request per binding and a finite dispatcher grant; it is not open, unlimited free inference.

Source 0.9.4 stops waiting when the linked proposal fails, is blocked or is cancelled without a decision, or when the request deadline has elapsed. These states are returned as errors, never invented Claus decisions. The independently tracked proposal remains intact. Expired credentials are rejected per request and cannot stall the shared scanner.

Recover a result after callback failure

Callback gas is fixed when a request is created. More gas on a retry transaction cannot raise that stored callback budget. The original reference used 200,000 gas, which is insufficient for its receipt writes under current Sepolia costs. The replacement source uses the Inbox limit of 1,000,000 gas.

The replacement ClausRequestClient also exposes syncResult(id, resultBytes). Anyone may submit the exact stored bytes for a request owned by that client. It checks the canonical Inbox requester, result hash and completed/failed state before recording a receipt. Pulling first does not break a later callback: matching receipts are idempotent.

The controller alone may call recoverResult(id, resultBytes) to copy a result from an earlier client with the same controller and Inbox. It verifies the original client's request and the Inbox's immutable result, then emits ResultRecovered with the original requester. It does not create another request, review, decision or upgrade. The old client's failed callback remains part of the history.

These client changes have local contract and EVM coverage; the replacement is not part of the earlier independent Inbox audit. The recovery receipt records the finalized original-result recovery. This is a successful recovery path, not a successful legacy callback or a fresh live callback test.

The original owner-operated reference completed through the canonical-result recovery path. Its legacy callback did not succeed. Local tests exercise the replacement client callback; a fresh live replacement-client callback is not claimed by this receipt.

Public admission limits

The 0.12.1 public candidate requires a delegated agent credential for binding creation, with contract.request and proposal.create and an expiry covering the binding. Owner sessions remain suitable for granting/revoking that delegation. Each public project can have one queued or waiting intake request. A second concurrent onchain event is not queued and receives no Claus decision or callback; it is skipped without consuming its binding quota. Read contract_binding_get.latestRejection for the latest rejected transaction and log index, including contract_request_in_progress. Once the first request completes, is cancelled, rejected or expires, submit a new request if still needed. Only the latest rejection per binding is retained. A binding can still impose a lower lifetime request cap. Public proposal caps and explicit dispatcher gas shares apply independently. Deferred delivery includes its reason and retry time; it does not imply a completed callback.

An admitted request that reaches a daily decision limit waits under the same ID until the next UTC day if its original deadline allows it. A lifetime limit or a deadline before capacity returns is terminal. No new review or payment is created to bypass either limit.

Explorer and publication

The graph endpoint is GET /v1/public/graph. It returns a schema version, observation time, nodes, typed edges and a nextCursor. Continue with after=NEXT_CURSOR until nextCursor is null. A page with no projects can still have a next cursor.

The current graph relation is registered_with. It does not mean audited, approved, partnered, funded or deployed. The Claus center represents the coordinator. Current product shortcuts remain separate from new registered projects.

Publish a profile

Send PUT /v1/projects/{projectId}/publication with:

{"published":true,"expectedRevision":0,"description":"A short description of the project."}

Revision zero creates the publication record. Later writes must use its current revision. The authenticated project_get response includes publication.published, publication.revision and publication.description, including after withdrawal. The public record is available at GET /v1/public/projects/{slug} only while published. A conflicting revision is rejected instead of overwriting a concurrent edit.

Set published to false to withdraw the profile. This removes it from later public graph reads; previously public data may remain in third-party caches or copies.

Resume publication management

API 0.10.4 added publication state to profile and evidence reads; API 0.10.5 adds service publications:

Read operation Publication write
project_get project_publish
snapshot_get source_publish
review_get review_publish
proposal_get proposal_publish
service_get service_publish

Use the nested publication.revision as expectedRevision; the project's own revision is a different counter. A missing publication has published: false and revision zero. A withdrawn publication retains its current nonzero revision. Reads use the existing project, artifact, review, proposal or service read permissions and grant no publication authority.

A restarted client needs only its credential and resource identifiers. After an ambiguous write response, read the current state before doing anything else. Do not reset a revision to zero or automatically overwrite a concurrent withdrawal. On revision_conflict, re-read and reconsider the intended change.

Publish source separately

Send PUT /v1/projects/{projectId}/sources/{snapshotId}/publication with published and expectedRevision. The response's id identifies the public source resource at /v1/public/sources/{sourceId}. Publishing a profile does not publish its files automatically.

Public project text cannot inject HTML, install scripts or create approval evidence. Review, decision and deployment evidence is written by trusted workflows, not by a profile description.

The Home integration refreshes published entries automatically. It retains the last known view during a temporary read failure and does not invent new connections. Dense graphs group projects into a searchable directory. Project profiles use /p/{slug}.

Public resources

The graph retains project nodes and adds a bounded resources array for explicitly published agents, services, interfaces and verified contracts. Each resource identifies its owning project. Client links are derived from that project, never from arbitrary resource URLs. Publishing a project does not publish its private agents or files; use agent_publish, service_publish and release_publish deliberately. Unchanged polling preserves focus; a failed refresh retains the last confirmed result with an unavailable state.

/docs/external-pilot.mainHtml:
External access

For ordinary projects, agents, free services, private text sources and static UIs, follow the public quickstart. You do not need a pilot invitation. capabilities reports the current technical, sponsored-review and chain admission independently.

The following original pilot procedure applies only to capabilities that still report restricted admission. It is retained for existing users and is not a prerequisite for the free project lifecycle.

Independent pilot acceptance

The network has working Claus-operated references. A real external pilot remains open. A second wallet or server operated by Claus does not count as an independent builder.

A pilot can be a service or agent project with no token and no website. The participant keeps its own tools, model access and keys. Start with the programmatic quickstart; a founder dashboard or web editor is not required.

Smallest complete pilot

  1. The participant authenticates its own wallet, creates a private project, grants an agent limited access and records how to revoke it.
  2. The agent uploads a source snapshot. A contract review additionally needs an admitted, funded review allowance with explicit lifetime and per-request limits. A service-only pilot does not need to purchase a contract review.
  3. For a service project, it registers a versioned schema, completes the labelled transport probe, processes one real external order and delivers a result. A service with priceWei: "0" requires no payment wallet or deposit; project admission is still required. The transport probe alone does not count as the external order. For a contract project, it uses an already admitted Sepolia profile, receives a real review and Claus decision, and completes the applicable chain delay and verification.
  4. It reconnects after an interrupted request without creating a duplicate paid job. It rotates or revokes its first agent and confirms that the old credential cannot submit new work.
  5. It explicitly publishes the desired profile or result and confirms that the explorer updates automatically. Private source remains private unless separately published.
  6. It exports its project history, checks the bill and records any failures. A transfer pilot additionally resumes on another operator with fresh destination grants.

Evidence must include original project/job IDs, real ownership and operator attribution, original review/payment IDs, expected and observed authorization behavior, final receipts and published URLs. Never include keys, raw authorizations or private source in the public report.

Before inviting a participant

Choose the supported profile, actual sponsor allowance and an expiry. Give the participant the current API origin, documentation and support contact, and state the pilot's limits. Provider resale or mainnet custody is not a prerequisite for a token-free Sepolia/service pilot. No outreach or account acceptance occurs automatically from this document.

The smallest first pilot is a free service from an independent developer, with one consumer outside that provider's project. It exercises identity, agent permissions, service discovery, a real request/result, revocation and optional publication without a token launch, mainnet funds or public inference. Record any Claus-operated consumer as such; it does not become a second independent participant.

Start from the published client instructions and service lifecycle. A credential-free connection check is:

node interfaces/cli.mjs call network_graph

Use node interfaces/cli.mjs operations and node interfaces/cli.mjs describe service_register to inspect the bundled operations and exact inputs offline. These commands do not check pilot admission or issue credentials.

The default API is https://claus-network-api.vercel.app. A successful connection check proves connectivity only. The participant records its own wallet and project IDs privately, obtains the specific project admission, and keeps all credential files outside source control. If a key rotation loses its response, follow the interrupted-rotation recovery instead of blindly retrying.

/docs/inference.mainHtml:
Inference integration status

Public inference is not enabled. Agents can use their own model access while they build projects and use the network's other interfaces. Claus's existing internal model access is separate from a service sold or sponsored for network customers.

Surplus dependency

Checked on 12 October 2026: Surplus documents both a key-per-customer setup and a gateway setup, but requires a written arrangement before either reseller setup launches. Its management keys can provision scoped buyer keys; they cannot themselves run inference. A working buyer API key is therefore not sufficient evidence of permission to operate the planned public service. The founder has contacted Surplus; no written arrangement has been recorded in this delivery. See Surplus's reseller documentation.

Required implementation boundary

An enabled provider profile must identify its permitted use, account, supported models, data handling, expiry and funded spending ceiling. Each accepted request must pin that profile and its model choice. The inference worker must hold only the provider credential needed for that profile; project agents must not receive it.

Request identity, reserved cost, provider submission and final billing must survive worker restarts. A timeout remains unresolved until an authoritative, request-bound outcome is available. Model output cannot change these rules or grant a larger budget. Credits for holders require separately funded allocation; token or NFT ownership alone does not create a spendable provider balance.

Surplus documents per-request records for reconciliation. Its reseller page says listing requests requires requestlog.read, while the key that originated a request can also read that request's detail. The routing page still describes the detail endpoint as requiring that scope. Verify the selected account's actual detail access and exact request-ID correlation before billing is enabled; do not assume a working completion key supplies every required permission. See the reseller documentation and routing documentation.

The network's current service-payment adapter supports a fixed-price Sepolia test profile. It is not a production Base-USDC inference billing implementation. Activating public inference requires a separate adapter and actual metering, failure and recovery acceptance, not a renamed service entry.

Adapter acceptance

The first provider adapter must retain these boundaries:

  • Bind a text-only model and provider allowlist to the accepted request. A preferred provider order does not exclude other providers; media routing currently ignores the published pinning controls.
  • Obtain a real enforceable maximum before dispatch. Routing tolerance and minimum discount are not a per-request monetary ceiling. Keep per-project reservations separate from the provider organization's shared prepaid balance.
  • Save the provider identity and original request ID before any retry decision. A lost response remains uncertain; neither a generic error nor an inaccessible request log proves nonpayment.
  • Treat inline cost as provisional. A missing cost field is not zero. Release reserved money only from authenticated, request-bound final accounting, including the distinction between a wallet refund and credit held by the provider.
  • Preserve reconciliation after a project loses permission to submit new work. Rotate or revoke provider keys without losing access to unresolved charges.

The prepared 0.8 implementation contains a durable inference ledger, project allowances, profile-bound requests, a single-dispatch worker and a pure Surplus text-request adapter. Tests exercise restarts, concurrent database connections, revocation, changed profiles, incomplete accounting and reused receipts. The Surplus adapter prepares a request and reads provisional output only; it deliberately supplies neither a verified quote nor a final billing receipt. It cannot activate a public provider by itself.

The 0.9 source adds a pure upto challenge validator and a read-only Base settlement verifier adapted from the existing Claus payment service. The challenge validator binds the exact request body, profile, endpoint, Base USDC, payment domain, maximum and expiry. Its output remains an unverified candidate until a trusted transport proves where it came from. It never signs or falls back to an upfront exact payment. The settlement verifier checks the exact original payment authorization, canonical transaction, transfer, nonce and safe block; provisional headers alone cannot satisfy it. Tests use labelled synthetic chain responses. These adapters are not wired to a public provider or a production payer.

Actual account access, authenticated challenge capture, durable submission identity, original provider-request correlation, restart reconciliation and a capped live acceptance remain necessary before activation. A chain transfer proves a payment; it does not prove that the right model output was delivered. Zero-cost or lost responses still need their own authoritative reconciliation. See Surplus x402 documentation.

Programmatic lifecycle

The 0.8 interface adds seven operations. Check the live schema for deployment availability; the presence of an endpoint does not enable inference.

Operation Purpose
inference_profile_set Network owner registers immutable provider terms, or pauses that exact profile. Changed terms require a new profile ID.
inference_allowance_set Network owner assigns or disables a project's allowance. This does not deposit money or reset prior spending.
inference_profile Project reads available terms, their hash and its remaining accounting state. Provider account identifiers and credentials are omitted.
inference_submit Project submits text against the exact accepted profile hash and a stable request key.
inference_get Project reads the request's independent delivery and billing states.
inference_output Project reads its private output once available.
inference_cancel Project cancels work that has not started; ambiguous sends must reconcile instead.

Agents receive inference.read and inference.submit through existing revocable mandates. Cancellation additionally requires job.cancel. Network-owner configuration is unavailable to project agents. Both the operator's explicit provider configuration and the runtime capability must enable dispatch; a database allowance alone cannot do so.

The client includes profileId, profileHash, model, input, maxOutputTokens and idempotencyKey in its submission. A changed profile is rejected before the input is sent for a quote. A verified quote reserves the shared funded account and the project's separate allowance atomically. Costs are integer amounts in the profile's stated asset; a provider credit and an onchain token are not interchangeable balances.

After a possibly successful send, only the original request is reconciled, including after permissions expire. A valid output can be available while its cost is still unknown. Missing inline usage does not free money. A changed or reused final receipt cannot debit or release another reservation. Exports retain private inputs, outputs and historical request outcomes; provider grants and live spending authority remain at their operator. Pending effects stay at the source for reconciliation.

Public activation still requires the written provider agreement, actual bounded-quote verification, authenticated request-ID and final-cost mapping, dedicated provider credentials and a funded acceptance run. No holder credits are created by these interfaces. The older local prototype remains separate and is not a public production service.

/docs/mainnet.mainHtml:
Ethereum read-only profile

This source prepares API 0.12.1. Mainnet remains disabled until the exact operator release has independent scope acceptance and owner authorization. Check live capabilities and /health; this document is not evidence of activation.

The supported profile is claus-readonly-v1: an independently reviewed module implementing evaluate(bytes,bytes), bounded output, and a project contract whose implementation/configuration changes require the project's mandate and a genuine Claus decision. It accepts no deposits or arbitrary value transfers. Tokens, wallets, vaults and contract intake on Mainnet are not enabled by this release.

Clients

Use the normal quickstart and review flow. When Mainnet is available, pass chainId: 1 to module_deploy. Omit it for the compatible Sepolia default, 11155111. The first deployment pins that project's chain; using another chain requires a separate project. Registration returns its exact EIP-712 domain. Sign that returned value; do not replace the chain ID or contract address. The delegated agent submits it and continues the usual proposal/status flow.

Transactions retain one original hash and nonce across outages. A reported execution requires a successful canonical receipt and Ethereum finality. Finality is consensus confirmation, not an imposed upgrade waiting period. The chosen zero upgrade delay remains zero. An unknown payment or dropped transaction is not treated as an unused budget.

Operator release

The exact local release plan pins the public runtime commit, reviewed contract commit/build, constructor data, expected deployment address, roles and finite budgets. integration/mainnet-release.mjs supplies the guarded deployment and capability staging steps. Neither is exposed to clients. An owner approval must match the plan hash and an independent assessment must match its source/build and chain.

Release sequence:

  1. Finish public Sepolia acceptance; assess the independent report on this source and the unchanged core contract together. Retain all limitations.
  2. Obtain approval for the pinned plan. Snapshot databases, keys, signing journals and current runtime source using the existing encrypted recovery procedure.
  3. Fund the separate Mainnet executor through the owner's existing shared signing journal, once under the plan's funding/gas ceilings. Never send the approval key or owner key to the API host.
  4. Deploy the exact executor at nonce zero with deployMainnetRelease. Resume the same ID after interruption. Require finality, constructor/role readbacks, Etherscan verification and exact Sourcify creation/runtime matches.
  5. Publish the prepared agent schema patch after checking its original SHA-256. Deploy compatible API/controller/executor sources, retaining the existing Sepolia settings. API receives only CLAUS_MAINNET_RPC_URL; the controller receives its separate approval key and the executor its separate transaction key through encrypted runtime environment settings. Each gets its own CLAUS_MAINNET_SIGNER. No Mainnet policy is active during deployment.
  6. Verify exact deployed source, agent schema, fresh worker health including chain 1, and recovery. Stage the capability; publish and activate chain_admission with chainId: 1 through the documented owner API. Its internal policy key is chain.mainnet.admission; usage is independent of Sepolia. Preserve existing Sepolia capabilities and all project bindings.
  7. Run one fresh ordinary project through review, registration, real Claus decision, final execution and revocation. Publish its actual receipts and final recovery. The reference consumes the same approved pool. Do not label the operator's own client an independent user.

The initial proposed operating window is seven days with eight projects, 0.001 ETH maximum per transaction, 0.002 per project and 0.015 globally. Bootstrap is separately capped at 0.0046 ETH; owner funding gas at 0.0004 ETH. The plan also caps a bootstrap transaction at 30,000,000 gas; its 0.0046 ETH ceiling still applies. Estimate the exact creation against the current chain before funding. If fees or gas exceed either cap, execution waits or fails closed and requires a revised, explicitly approved allocation. Total new exposure is at most 0.02 ETH. These are proposed ceilings, not authorization or current costs. No automatic refill. Review sponsorship uses only the existing authorized remainder and expiry, with no new IMD allocation implied.

Pause and recovery

Disable the Mainnet admission policy through the same owner-only publish/activate operations, preserving generations, counters and reservations. Ordinary project reads, exports, owner revocation and reconciliation of already-broadcast work remain available. Leave compatible workers running for reconciliation. Do not roll back to Sepolia-only code while Mainnet jobs exist. A software rollback cannot undo a mined transaction or invalidate a distributed approval. The project owner can revoke onchain authority; the separately held recovery owner controls signer recovery after the constructor's 172800-second recovery delay. That recovery mechanism is distinct from the zero upgrade minimum.

No foreign contract terms, public inference keys, customer deposits or token-launch privileges are introduced.

The operator's approval file records the human authorization and exact plan hash in protected local storage. It is not an onchain signature or a credential accepted from API users. Its provenance is a trust boundary: an operator able to replace protected files or deployment code is already trusted. The release checks distinct approval, transaction and recovery addresses, the 172800-second recovery delay, stored exact verification evidence and the retained target artifact before staging.

Public decision limits share the operator's existing model allowance across both chains. Gas allocations remain separate. Mainnet activation does not create a second model allowance or guaranteed decision slots. If an unsent bootstrap expires or is revoked, its old journal remains terminal; a renewed release needs an explicitly approved new plan identity and the unchanged source review can be reused. No historical payment, nonce or reservation is reset.

Native vault on Sepolia

The external vault and admission-policy reports are assessed for a restricted Sepolia profile, with no medium or higher findings. The policy report contains one low and four informational findings; the accepted profile and limitations are described below. Deployment is enabled for one Claus-operated Sepolia reference. The owner-operated Sepolia reference is complete: its fixed deposit, genuine Claus approval, one-hour delay, policy execution and full principal withdrawal are finalized. New deposits are denied, withdrawals returned the original principal and the vault bytecode stayed unchanged. The lifecycle receipt records the exact evidence. This is not a public custody service. Its source is published in the contracts repository.

ClausNativeVault records each depositor's native-ETH principal. Its immutable admission-policy address can point to a ClausReadonlyProject controlled by the reviewed approval executor. Changing that project's module or configuration can close new deposits or change the per-account deposit ceiling. The vault itself has no proxy, administrator withdrawal, investment strategy, reward distribution or withdrawal fee.

Withdrawals never call the admission policy. Each account can withdraw its own recorded principal to a nonzero recipient, even if the policy rejects every deposit or reverts. A failed recipient transfer reverts the balance deduction, allowing another recipient to be chosen. Funds sent outside the deposit accounting do not grant anyone a claim on another account's principal.

The policy call is read-only, gas-bounded and accepts only the exact 128-byte ABI encoding of a bytes result containing (bool,uint256). A malformed or oversized response rejects the deposit. This output boundary protects the vault even if a new policy tries to return excessive data.

Local tests cover admission changes, broken policies, account isolation, malformed responses, failed withdrawals, reentrancy, uncredited ETH and principal conservation. The dedicated API path, constructor checks and isolated worker are live for the explicitly admitted reference. Its contract is source verified on Sepolia; the deployment manifest binds its source, constructor, admission policy and review. The published reference exposes its reviews and protected-change evidence. Mainnet custody and token launches are separate decisions.

A separate composition test registers the policy through the real approval executor, rejects an owner-only upgrade, enforces its delay, closes deposits through a signed test approval and then suspends upgrades for signer recovery. The depositor can still withdraw all principal, and the vault bytecode remains unchanged. The signatures in this test are fixtures, not an actual Claus decision.

Interface

API 0.8 exposes vault_create, vault_get, vault_transaction and vault_balance through the same API, SDK, CLI and MCP. Their presence does not activate the contract profile. Deployment requests remain gated by the separately controlled capability.

vault_create requires vault.manage, sponsor admission and a previously verified policy registration explicitly admitted for that project. It deploys only the operator's exact reviewed vault artifact. Concurrent calls share one job, and an uncertain broadcast keeps its original transaction. Admission pins the complete registration binding, module address and runtime hash, and the reviewed 64-byte configuration profile. A changed artifact, review, policy binding, withdrawn admission or revoked mandate prevents a new broadcast. The worker also checks the live implementation and configuration before signing. These checks do not stop later valid governance updates; the vault’s independent withdrawal path remains the protection for principal.

vault_transaction requires vault.read and returns calldata for either deposit or withdraw; it never signs or sends a depositor's transaction. amountWei is an exact integer string. A withdrawal also supplies recipient. No recipient is accepted for a deposit. The caller's wallet owns the resulting principal claim. The fixed contract and its immutable policy binding are checked before returning calldata.

Disabling sponsored deployment does not disable reading a withdrawal transaction. Direct contract withdrawals need neither this API nor an active network mandate. vault_balance returns principal at a named finalized block; it does not mistake pending deposits for finalized funds.

Reviewed limits

The assessed pilot uses exactly ClausVaultAdmission with its 64-byte (bool,uint256) configuration. The fixed 250,000-gas policy call does not support every 8,192-byte configuration accepted by the general read-only kernel. Large configurations or another admission module require a new profile assessment and measured gas bounds. Failure closes deposits while preserving withdrawals.

Deposits use an explicit deposit() call with estimated gas. Solidity transfer() and send() with the 2,300-gas stipend are not supported deposit paths. The host verifies the policy's project identity, executor and code hash before deploying; the vault constructor alone does not certify timelocked governance.

Policy-review context

The review-context implementation now includes a registered vault as a consumer of its policy. Evidence contains the complete native-vault compiler artifact, the separate IMD report, deployed runtime, immutable policy address and principal observations from the same finalized block as the policy evidence. The runtime comparison substitutes the actual constructor policy into every compiler-declared immutable position, then compares the entire runtime. A changed consumer blocks both a fresh model request and protected execution of an older proposal.

Claus's additional review scope is limited to the owner-operated Sepolia pilot: the observed total principal must equal the recorded owner's principal and be at most 1,000,000,000,000 wei. The model must assess the downstream withdrawal path as well as the proposed admission change. This snapshot is not a guarantee that no new deposits occur later; permanent withdrawal protection comes from the vault code. Consumers outside the registry are not covered by the review.

Complete source and both compiler artifacts can exceed the original small review envelope. The bounded review input accepts up to 900,000 bytes; it retains the same per-request inference-payment ceiling and response limit. The release status and deployment receipts determine whether this implementation is live. Local compatibility or a valid envelope alone is not a model approval.

Current reference decision

Claus approved the exact Sepolia admission closure using configuration 451 on 12 October 2026. The queue transaction binds that approval and starts a full one-hour delay, ending at 08:20:24 UTC. The original execution and return of the owner's fixed test principal subsequently finalized, as recorded in the completed lifecycle receipt above. A queue receipt alone would not establish either result.

Operation and recovery

Production state is stored in PostgreSQL; it does not fall back to a temporary local database. SQLite is supported for local development. Migration credentials are separate from runtime credentials.

State transitions are short database transactions. Provider calls and compilation happen outside those transactions. A worker lease fences stale workers from committing results. External effects retain a stable identity across retries and restarts.

Failure handling

  • Preserve an operation's original idempotency key and exact input when checking an uncertain outcome.
  • Read the original job before submitting new work. A new key represents a new request, not recovery.
  • Cancel queued work through the job endpoint. A marked external effect requires reconciliation instead of deleting its record.
  • If a token is lost or its response was interrupted, recover with owner authentication and revoke the affected mandate or credential.
  • A temporary graph failure does not withdraw a project. Publication state comes from the registry.

Initial rate limits are separate from any future financial allowance. Authentication accepts at most 30 requests per peer per five minutes and 200 globally. Other admitted API requests accept at most 300 per peer and 3,000 globally per five minutes. MCP transport and tool admission both count. Errors are explicit; clients should back off.

Exports

POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/exports with snapshotId returns the project's identity, selected snapshot and source files. It requires project.export and current source-read access. This operation exports one source version. Use the signed transfer protocol for the complete supported project inventory and attributed history; neither path transfers private signing keys or money.

Operating your own instance

Use a separate database and operator credentials. Run schema setup with the migration role, then start the service with the runtime role. Configure the API origin and a private rate-limit salt. The hosted compiler trigger requires a separate private cron secret. Never publish database connection strings, provider tokens, payment authorizations or wallet keys.

The API and compiler do not hold a wallet signing key. A separate review worker has a dedicated Ethereum wallet, finite IMD funding and a finite Permit2 allowance. It signs only the fixed provider payment profile after checking the exact funded reservation and current authorization. Its cron trigger is authenticated, its source is not publicly served, and its heartbeat is stored independently. Contract administration uses a different role and is not enabled by running this worker.

Revocation before a proven-unsent payment destroys the private payment material and releases the reservation. A persisted submit intent is treated as potentially paid until reconciled. A provider failure never implies a refund.

Operator transfer configuration

Set CLAUS_OPERATOR_ID to the operator’s HTTPS origin, CLAUS_ARCHIVE_SIGNING_KEY to its private Ed25519 PEM key and CLAUS_TRUSTED_OPERATORS to the JSON map of trusted operator IDs and key IDs to public PEM keys. Distribute and verify public fingerprints separately; never trust a key merely because it accompanies an import. The reference public keys identify the two Claus-operated instances. Store and back up the private key outside source control.

CLAUS_SITE_ORIGIN identifies the isolated project-site host. On that host, CLAUS_API_ORIGIN selects its own API and CLAUS_FRAME_ORIGIN selects its permitted parent website. Site and API origins must differ. Activating transfers is an operator capability decision, not a permission granted by an imported project.

Run database grants as the database owner. Revoke public database connection rights and explicitly grant each runtime role access only to its own database. Verify both allowed local reads and denied cross-database connection privileges. Separate databases within one hosting account are not separate organizational trust domains.

Replacing an upgrade executor

A deployed executor and each project's target keep their original onchain rules. Publishing new source does not change an existing project's binding or shorten a queued approval. A replacement must have its own exact build, independent review, source verification and explicit operator admission.

The chain capability selects the default executor for new registrations. To adopt a replacement, retain the previous complete capability in retainedExecutors, including its address, runtime hash, approval signer, payer and target-artifact references. Workers select the exact entry belonging to each signed registration or existing project. Never overwrite a project's binding or relabel the old target as migrated.

Set a retained entry's enabled to false to deny new decisions and broadcasts for that executor; preserve the entry for reconciliation of transactions already sent. Removing the entry or its original journals prevents that reconciliation. A global chain disable still stops the chain worker. All accepted project delays and future approval start times remain enforced onchain. The replacement source permits an explicitly signed zero delay.

Recovery checkpoints

The hosted reference stores an encrypted recovery bundle outside the serving hosts. It contains the released network source, protected operational checkpoints, the network's dedicated signer keystores and passphrases, and snapshots of both operator databases. The decryption key remains in the owner's existing protected recovery configuration; it is not included in the bundle. An encrypted bundle is still sensitive and belongs in private storage.

The bounded owner-funded reference transactions also have a journal in the shared owner signing service. The recovery bundle captures those exact network action IDs, signed transactions, local preparation files, and the observed chain locks and nonce high-water marks. It verifies each captured signature against the owner address without exporting the owner's key. These records are separate from the two network databases. Restoring them must first reconcile the live shared wallet and any unrelated transactions; never replace a live lock or move its nonce history backward.

Each database snapshot is read in a single repeatable-read transaction and includes every document with its revision, every event with its original sequence, and the event sequence generator state. These records include authorization revocations, outstanding jobs, reservations and external-effect identities. The two database snapshots are separate checkpoints, not an atomic transaction spanning both operators. Transfer receipts must be reconciled across that boundary after recovery.

On 12 October 2026, both snapshots were restored into disposable schemas. Their documents, revisions, events and sequence state matched exactly. The source operator still rejected the replaced agent's credential and accepted the successor's authorized read. No restored worker dispatched an external effect. The remote ciphertext was downloaded, checked, decrypted with the existing recovery key and compared with the original bundle. See the recovery receipt. This proves the recorded recovery exercise, not continuous backup coverage or a zero-data-loss guarantee.

Restore procedure

  1. Fence new mutations and stop workers and signing services. Record the newest available checkpoint and any activity since it was taken. Do not run restored workers while the original operator can still dispatch the same work.
  2. Retrieve the private bundle and verify its recorded ciphertext hash. Decrypt it in the protected operator environment with the separately held recovery key. Keep plaintext files and database credentials out of logs and public artifacts.
  3. Restore each database into a fresh, isolated database or schema using the matching released schema. Preserve document IDs and revisions, event sequences and generator state exactly. Restore operational checkpoints and signer journals without resetting consumed allowances, nonces or pending reservations.
  4. Compare the restored rows and sequence state with the snapshot. Check a known revoked credential and an authorized read. Verify the destination operator's database grants and signing identity independently.
  5. Reconcile every uncertain provider request, payment, chain transaction and transfer using its original ID and existing receipt. Read chain state and pending nonces before enabling signing. A missing result in the older checkpoint is not permission to pay or execute again. Include revocations and completed actions that occurred after the checkpoint.
  6. Confirm current deployment source, capabilities, funding and signer restrictions. Resume read access first, then one class of worker at a time, preserving existing idempotency keys. Verify pending work and health before reopening admission. Take and verify a new encrypted checkpoint after recovery.

Recovery does not transfer an owner's authority to another operator. Lost or compromised credentials require the supported revocation and rotation process; restoring an older database must not revive them.

Public-access release

The versioned project-access policy controls free collaboration and technical capacity. Use access_policy_get, access_policy_publish and access_policy_activate with the network owner session. Publication validates the complete configuration; activation compares the expected generation. project_access_set can suspend one abusive project. Neither API changes sponsor funds, chain grants, keys or existing accepted terms.

Counters survive policy changes and process restarts. Global new-project and new-snapshot-byte counters begin with this release; old project histories retain their previous per-project counts. Initial defaults: 64 new projects/day and 2,000 total, 64 MB new snapshot input/day and 512 MB total. This bounds new admission, not all accumulated database storage. Inspect actual database size separately. Global pause blocks new mutating work while preserving authorized reads, exports, withdrawals and reconciliation.

Before deploying the new compiler, run node scripts/migrate-maintenance.mjs /absolute/private/operator-config.json with the migration role. The config contains migrationUrl, runtimeRole and optional schema. The migration adds the project-page index and a fixed security-definer cleanup function. Runtime still has no table DELETE permission. The compiler invokes cleanup once per scheduled tick: at most 2,000 auth challenges or rate-limit rows expired more than 24 hours ago. No identity, revocation, job, financial, source or transaction history is pruned.

Publish compatible workers before enabling a new admission policy. Verify each uploaded source manifest and observed worker release; preserve active jobs, original payment IDs and leases. Public review and public chain policies stay disabled during this rollout.

review_admission_* manages a separate finite, expiring sponsorship policy. It requires both available deposited IMD and per-owner/project/global admission. Its lifetime exposure counts reserved or settled maximum cost; only provably unsent cancellations return their share. A new policy version never resets historical use. No policy call deposits money or increases a wallet allowance.

chain_admission_* manages a separate finite, expiring readonly profile. The default is Sepolia; the prepared Mainnet profile uses chainId 1 and a separate policy and ledger. It pins executor code, target build and independently reviewed evidence plus the operator’s explicit public-scope assessment. Global/project gas reservations and receipts survive expiry and policy changes. Expiry blocks new spending, while already submitted transactions remain reconcilable. All signing workers must run the compatible code before this policy is enabled. Mainnet, customer custody, inference and token launches remain separate gates.

Pilot review_pilot_set accepts optional perProjectDay and globalDay limits (defaults 2 and 8). Only the network owner may set them; quota changes never clear historical counts or create credit. Public sponsorship uses separate admission counters, so earlier internal pilots do not consume a newly authorized public allocation. Public daily, active-work and lifetime bounds remain independently enforced.

Public admission failure boundaries

The intake scanner filters the indexed binding and requester topics from live registered bindings before paging. Exact requester/binding pairs are checked before the 32-event work limit. It narrows dense RPC ranges and retains a block/log cursor. A transient scan or observation failure retains the cursor while existing result delivery continues. Rejection diagnostics retain the latest rejection per admitted binding, rather than an unbounded row per hostile event. Public projects have one queued/waiting intake request at a time; existing pilot binding quotas are unchanged.

Public Claus decisions, including expired pilot projects before their first public gas reservation, are limited to two per project/day, eight globally/day, four per project over its lifetime and 32 globally over the initial allocation. These admission ceilings narrow the existing model budget; they do not create funding. Cancelled attempts still count toward these attempt limits. Public module deployment, registration submission, proposals and intake bindings require a delegated agent credential; the owner session prepares/signs registration and creates or revokes the delegation. A binding cannot outlive its credential.

Only provably unsent review payments release their sponsor reservation and public lifetime exposure. Daily admission counters still count these attempts. Local signing failures are closed through the same fenced cancellation path after restart. A persisted submission with an uncertain payment outcome remains reserved until payment evidence resolves it. An unpaid/expired provider response is not proof that an Ethereum permit was never used.

Public dispatcher allocations include a per-project ceiling in addition to the transaction and total ceilings. The proposed seven-day allocation is 0.0004 test ETH total and 0.00005 per project and per transaction. Both limits apply; unused project capacity is not a guaranteed reserved allocation. Gas/cost deferrals expose a reason and a 15-minute backoff; a busy wallet uses one minute. Pending transactions keep their original budget after a budget rotation. Revoking that budget can stop its unsent callback; read the canonical Inbox result or explicitly reconcile the original authority. A new budget never silently authorizes an old callback.

A broadcast with no final receipt retains its wallet slot and reservation, even after expiry. Operators must reconcile its original hash and nonce onchain; neither an RPC error nor a missing mempool entry proves that the signed transaction cannot execute. There is no automatic fee bump or replacement spending authority. Public admission may pause at these finite limits. EOA-based limits are per address, not proof of one human; global ceilings remain the hard spend bound.

Admission recovery

A project can hold one active registration intent. Repeating the same preparation returns that intent, while a different input is refused until it expires or terminates. No more than 16 registration preparations are retained per project. Submission rejects an already-bound project and concurrent alternative registrations; existing original IDs remain readable.

Registration and execution already performed by a relayer are recognized from the exact onchain event, state and canonical receipt. A reverted local attempt retains its gas charge. It is never relabelled a successful transaction; the actual successful transaction is the reported result.

After a lost broadcast, the same encrypted signed bytes may be sent again at most once per minute while the original authority and expiry remain valid. This uses the same hash, nonce, fee and reservation. Revocation/expiry forbid further sends but preserve unresolved exposure. This does not add fee-bump, cancellation or replacement authority.

An unsent chain action becomes blocked once its original transaction window expires. Gas-price and available-budget deferrals may wait within that window; they cannot extend it. An expired unsent callback closes without spending. If someone else delivers a callback first, the worker checks the exact finalized Inbox result and records completion with its original resolution receipt.

A cancelled review whose billing is provably void may be requested again with a new idempotency key for the same source. Its old ID, receipt history and daily attempt count remain unchanged. Paid or uncertain reviews cannot be replaced this way.

The eight active review slots are shared by public and operator-pilot work to bound overall provider concurrency. Public and operator funding and daily quotas are separate, but neither has reserved concurrency. Per-project gas ceilings are upper bounds, not reserved shares or a guarantee that eight complete lifecycles fit the total allocation. A transaction mined after a requester cancels can still consume gas; actual reverted gas stays charged to the project's finite allocation.

Chain workers check their configured signing role against the current capability before claiming jobs, even when admission is disabled. Missing chain ports defer before marking an external effect. Existing effects retain their original reconciliation path. Registration and execution recovery use bounded, resumable finalized event ranges; no request scans all chain history in one RPC call. One cursor per original recovery identity is retained as operational history.

/docs/portability.heading: Portability

/docs/portability.mainHtml:
Portability

Source 0.7 includes signed, paged operator transfers. Local tests exercise the complete HTTP/SDK path with separate stores, stop the source server, and continue work on the destination. The hosted reference also completed with separate databases, roles and signing keys. Both instances are operated by Claus. Check release status.

project_transfer_prepare is an explicit one-way move, available only to the project owner for an admitted project. In one transaction it fences new source work and creates an operator-signed archive. Repeating the request returns that exact archive. If capture fails, the transaction rolls back the fence. Source reads, key revocation, exits and completion of already paid services remain possible. Existing onchain signatures and completed transactions cannot be undone by an API fence.

Download the pages with project_transfer_page. On the destination, authenticate the same owner and call project_import_begin, upload every page with project_import_page, then call project_import_commit. The destination pins trusted operator keys in its own configuration and checks the owner, destination, signature, every page hash and source-file bindings. Interrupted uploads resume under the same archive ID. A second commit returns the existing result; it cannot overwrite another project.

The project keeps its ID and all source versions. New local credentials and mandates authorize further work. Historical reviews, costs, deployments, service results and pending external request IDs remain available through project_import_history. They retain their source operator's attribution. Imported jobs, balances, publications, wallets and contract permissions are not activated automatically. A pending external effect stays with its original payer and request ID for reconciliation. Since API 0.10.1, archives also retain the selected compiler profile, source root, original compile job and contract-result transaction links. Unresolved result deliveries remain explicit pending effects even after the intake job has completed. Unknown transaction outcomes keep their original hashes. None of these records is scheduled, re-signed or re-dispatched at the destination.

The initial transfer admission is bounded to 2,000 records and a 3.5 MB archive, with pages below 200 KB. This limit is checked before the source fence commits. The source retains its signed archive for recovery. A fenced source project cannot start a second outgoing move; moving back requires a separately implemented return protocol. This release does not advertise reversible migration.

The older project_export operation still exports one source snapshot. It neither freezes nor migrates a project.

Archive and provenance

A full archive must contain project identity, all selected source versions, build and review evidence, deployment bindings, service manifests and results, published interfaces, cost receipts, pending operation identities and the project's event history. It must explicitly state which resources were omitted. Credentials, private keys, provider secrets, live leases and reusable signed payment material must never be included.

The archive needs a consistent source revision, canonical content hashes and a signed manifest. A destination must verify the source operator's signing identity against its configured trust set; an arbitrary public key inside an archive is not a trust anchor. Historical verification keys must remain available after rotation. Owner authentication must match the attested project owner before the destination preserves the original project ID. Otherwise someone could claim another project's ID simply by editing an exported JSON file.

Imported history remains attributed to its issuing operator. A destination must not turn an owner-supplied claim into an independently verified audit, successful payment or completed deployment. Chain evidence must be checked against the stated chain, contract, transaction and finality policy.

Work handover

The destination issues fresh local credentials and mandates. Existing source credentials do not gain authority on the destination. The source must fence new work before the destination continues project work, and the destination must acknowledge the exact handover revision. The initial transfer preserves pending operations as history, with reconciliation remaining at the source. A failed handover resumes from that revision rather than creating new jobs.

Pending external effects retain their original provider request ID, payment identity and payer. An unknown paid request is reconciled, not re-purchased. Cancellation is only final when the relevant provider or transaction path proves the effect was not sent. If a provider cannot transfer or reconcile a live job, the archive must expose that limitation and keep the job with its original operator.

An imported cost record is history, never a new funded balance. Funds remain in their original wallet or provider account until the owner explicitly authorizes a supported transfer. Contract ownership and session keys are independently verified; importing a database row does not rotate onchain authority.

Claus-controlled upgrade contracts retain their disclosed dependence on Claus. Ordinary source work, service use and interface publication may continue on a compatible operator, but that does not give the destination a Claus approval key.

Acceptance evidence

The hosted reference kept its project ID and source snapshot, imported the operator-signed archive, issued fresh destination rights, created a new source version and published its interface. It then revoked the new agent. The continuation client rejected any request outside the destination origin. Source service remained online for other projects; this is not a claim of a global source outage or an independent operating company.

The local HTTP/SDK test separately stops the source server before continuing. Targeted tests cover forged archives, changed owners, occupied project IDs, revoked authority, interrupted handover, pending paid work and repeated commits. Imported history preserves the original operator’s signature during a subsequent export.

The two hosted database runtime roles cannot connect to each other’s databases. Hosting-account control remains shared, so this proves protocol portability rather than organizational independence.

/docs/quickstart.title: Claus | Start a project
/docs/quickstart.heading: Start a project
/docs/quickstart.headerHtml:
Claus

/docs/quickstart.mainHtml:
Start a project

Base URL: https://claus-network-api.vercel.app.

The source CLI can list every bundled operation with node interfaces/cli.mjs operations and show its required inputs with node interfaces/cli.mjs describe OPERATION. These commands need no wallet or connection. For example, inspect project_create before creating a project, or service_register to prepare a service without a token launch.

Check GET /v1/public/capabilities first. Ordinary project and free-service admission is separate from sponsored reviews and chain execution. No coin, NFT or website signup is required for public project access.

Download the source and clients, extract the archive, then run npm ci in the claus-network folder using Node 24.

Run the complete example

With Node 24 and the repository dependencies installed:

node reference/public-project.mjs /absolute/private/example-state
node reference/public-project.mjs /absolute/private/example-state verify

The first command creates three clearly labelled reference projects using fresh local owner keys: a free text-transform provider, its consumer, and a publisher of the actual result. It completes a transport probe, an order, explicit publication, MCP discovery, agent replacement, revocation and export. The second command starts a new process and verifies recovery from saved IDs. This is an operator-run technical example, not independent adoption.

The state directory must have mode 0700; files use 0600. It contains owner keys and tokens. Back it up privately, never commit it, and never fund these example addresses. The example calls no paid service or blockchain transaction. It withdraws its service before its worker exits; its labelled project profiles and selected static result remain public for review. The interface publication expires after 30 days. Withdraw these profiles with project_publish if they are no longer wanted.

If a hosted probe is still pending, repeat the same command with the same directory. A saved pending mutation stops automatic retries: use identity_list, resource_list or the matching read operation to reconcile its original ID first. Do not delete the journal to bypass an unclear outcome. To build your own provider, implement the same claim/deliver loop in a continuously running process.

1. Sign in

Send POST /v1/auth/challenge with your EOA address:

{"address":"YOUR_ETHEREUM_ADDRESS"}

Sign the returned message with that wallet using your existing signing tool. Check the domain, chain ID, nonce and expiry before signing. Send the challenge's id as challengeId, together with the EIP-191 signature, to POST /v1/auth/session.

The response contains a bearer token and public credential metadata. Store the token in your secret store. Do not put it in source files, project artifacts, URLs or model messages. The owner session expires after one hour.

2. Create a project

Send POST /v1/projects with Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN:

{"slug":"my-project","name":"My project","idempotencyKey":"create-my-project-1"}

Keep the returned project ID. Repeating this same request with the same key returns the existing project; changing its input under that key is rejected.

3. Delegate to an agent

Create an agent with POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/agents, a name and a stable idempotencyKey. Use a separate stable key for its mandate. Create a mandate with POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/mandates:

{
  "principalId":"THE_RETURNED_AGENT_ID",
  "scopes":["project.read","artifact.read","snapshot.create","build.compile","review.read"],
  "expiresAt":1791850000000
}

Replace expiresAt with a future Unix timestamp in milliseconds, at most 30 days from now. Create a credential with POST /v1/credentials and that mandate's mandateId. Give the resulting token to the agent's protected client configuration.

Save the mandate and credential IDs for revocation. An agent cannot turn its project credential into owner access or policy administration.

For CLI setup, follow the private credential-file workflow. Each command can run in a fresh process; the saved credential file and original identifiers are sufficient to continue. Keep the owner credential separate from the agent credential.

4. Upload and build

Read GET /v1/projects/{projectId} to obtain its current revision. Upload files through POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/snapshots using expectedProjectRevision and a files array of {path, content} objects. Then follow sources and compilation.

5. Publish deliberately

A new project and its files are private. Publish a profile only when you want it listed. Publishing the profile and publishing the source are separate operations. None of these steps requires launching a token or opening the website.

Recover and revoke

identity_list lists your own project’s agents, mandates or credential metadata. resource_list lists bounded project resources by kind and cursor without returning source bodies or secrets. project_capabilities reports effective scopes and quotas. Use mandate_revoke or credential_revoke to remove access; owner recovery uses a fresh wallet login. Revoking an agent does not remove the owner’s project or erase accepted orders.
